cost-of-living.name: Rising costs
cost-of-living.line: Everything costs more each year, and my pay hasn't kept up.
cost-of-living.why: Says what inflation feels like in a day, keeps the pay gap from the alias, and the name matches what the ID names.

cost-of-living.name: Inflation
cost-of-living.line: I can't keep up as prices rise faster than my pay.
cost-of-living.why: Keeps the familiar name and adds the pay side, which is what makes rising prices hurt.

it-all-goes-up.name: Inequality
it-all-goes-up.line: I see the gap between people with plenty and people who are struggling keep growing.
it-all-goes-up.why: Same meaning, fixes the awkward "those struggling grow" so the sentence reads naturally out loud.

it-all-goes-up.name: Growing gap
it-all-goes-up.line: I see the people who own things get more while everyone else falls behind.
it-all-goes-up.why: Brings back the earlier wording people recognized, in plainer words than "inequality".

ai-and-jobs.name: AI job losses
ai-and-jobs.line: I worry AI will replace people's jobs and no one has a plan for them.
ai-and-jobs.why: Names the problem rather than the technology, matching the ID, and says what "no one's ready" means.

ai-and-jobs.name: AI and jobs
ai-and-jobs.line: I worry AI will take people's work and no one's ready for it.
ai-and-jobs.why: A light touch: the name says what about AI worries people, and the line keeps its voice.

no-floor.name: No safety net
no-floor.line: If I lose my job or get sick, I know there's nothing to fall back on.
no-floor.why: Says what falling means in a day instead of a metaphor, and the name states the problem so it matches the heading's other problem names.

childcare-costs.name: Childcare costs
childcare-costs.line: I can't afford childcare, even though I need it to work.
childcare-costs.why: The name says the problem is the cost, and the line adds the bind most parents describe.

rent-eats-everything.name: High rent
rent-eats-everything.line: Rent takes so much of my pay that little is left for anything else.
rent-eats-everything.why: Brings back the ID's "rent eats everything" in plain words, and the name states the problem.

cant-afford-kids.name: Can't afford kids
cant-afford-kids.line: I want kids but can't afford to raise them.
cant-afford-kids.why: The earlier name says the problem plainly, where "Starting a family" reads like a topic, and it matches the ID.

pairs.distinction: Rising prices squeeze my own budget; inequality is the gap between groups, which can grow even when prices are steady.
pairs.reason: Someone hit by prices and someone angry about the rich pulling away are naming different things, and either could pick one without the other.

pairs.distinction: Rent is one bill; rising costs are everything at once, from groceries to gas.
pairs.reason: Housing is the biggest cost for many people and deserves its own pain, while rising prices covers the rest of the budget.

pairs.distinction: One is not having children because of cost; the other is paying for care for children you already have.
pairs.reason: A person choosing whether to have kids and a parent paying a daycare bill are in different places, so each would pick one easily.

pairs.distinction: Rent is about the cost of housing for anyone; starting a family is about putting off kids, often because of housing.
pairs.reason: Housing costs are one reason people put off kids, but the pain someone names is either the rent or the family they can't start.

pairs.distinction: Rent is my own bill being too high; homelessness is seeing neighbors who have no home at all.
pairs.reason: Paying too much and having nowhere to live are different situations, even though high rent drives homelessness.

pairs.distinction: The safety net is about having nothing to catch you; homelessness is one place people land without it.
pairs.reason: A person worried about one bad month is naming something wider than people sleeping outside.
Being short on money is personal and rising prices is the shared cause, so the same squeeze shows up on both pages and the two should stay linked.

pairs.distinction: Inequality is the gap in money and wealth; opportunity is whether where you start decides where you end up.
pairs.reason: They often travel together, but someone can be bothered by the wealth gap today without naming mobility, and the other way around.

pairs.distinction: Childcare is the bill; parenting is being worn out by the work of raising kids.
pairs.reason: A parent who can't pay for daycare and a parent who is exhausted are naming different problems, even if both are true at once.
Student debt is a common kind of the debt people carry personally, so it belongs on both pages as two pains linked across them.

pairs.distinction: Rent is what housing costs; housing on the personal page is the state of the place, cramped, broken or noisy.
pairs.reason: Paying too much and living somewhere in bad shape are different complaints, and many people have only one of them.
High rent is the shared cause and fear of eviction is how it lands for one household, so the two stay linked across pages.
Seeing neighbors without a home and fearing I'll lose mine are the same issue seen from the street and from inside, so they stay linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: AI is one specific cause of job loss across society; layoffs is my own job being at risk for any reason.
pairs.reason: Someone worried about their own layoff may not be thinking about AI at all, and someone worried about AI may feel secure in their own job.

pairs.distinction: AI is a worry about jobs disappearing in the future; unemployment is not finding work now.
pairs.reason: One is a fear about where work is heading and the other is a present search, so a person can tell them apart at once.

pairs.distinction: The safety net covers any fall, from job loss to illness; medical bills are the cost of care itself.
pairs.reason: Medical bills are one way people fall, but the worry about healthcare costs stands on its own under health.
Seeing people near me go hungry and worrying my own food won't last are the same issue at two scales, so they stay linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: Decline is the town losing jobs, shops and people; neighbors is not knowing the people who are still here.
pairs.reason: A thriving city can be full of strangers and a shrinking town can be close-knit, so these are different losses.

pairs.distinction: Decline is the town emptying out; local control is who makes the decisions about it.
pairs.reason: Decisions made far away can be one cause of decline, but someone watching shops close is naming the loss, not the governance.

no-cushion.name: No savings
no-cushion.line: I couldn't cover a surprise bill if one came.
no-cushion.why: Brings the wording back to the cushion the ID names, says what having nothing put aside looks like in a day, and makes the name a problem like Broke and Debt.

no-cushion.name: No savings
no-cushion.line: I have nothing put aside if something goes wrong.
no-cushion.why: Keeps the original line almost as it was and only adds when the missing savings would matter; the name becomes a problem like Broke and Debt.

cant-stop-working.name: Can't retire
cant-stop-working.line: I won't have enough to stop working when I'm older.
cant-stop-working.why: Says the worry the ID names, never being able to stop working, in plain words, and makes the name a problem like Broke and Debt instead of an area.

cant-stop-working.name: Can't retire
cant-stop-working.line: I'll have to keep working because I won't have enough to retire.
cant-stop-working.why: Keeps the original line's retirement wording and adds what it means for the person; the name becomes a problem like Broke and Debt.

running-out-of-food.name: Not enough food
running-out-of-food.line: I worry the food won't last until my next paycheck.
running-out-of-food.why: Says plainly what the pain is, matching the problem names Broke and Debt, and ties the line to a moment people know instead of the calendar month.

running-out-of-food.name: Not enough food
running-out-of-food.line: I worry the food won't last the month.
running-out-of-food.why: Keeps the original line, which is already plain, and only changes the area name Food into a problem name like Broke and Debt.

broke.name: Broke
broke.line: I run out of money before my next paycheck.
broke.why: Says what being always short looks like, so it reads less like Debt or No savings and more like the month-to-month squeeze.

pairs.distinction: Broke is not having enough money coming in for what this month costs; Debt is what you already owe and can't pay down.
pairs.reason: Plenty of people are short each month without big debts, and plenty carry debts on a decent income, so they'd pick one without hesitating.

pairs.distinction: Broke is about getting through this month; No savings is about having nothing if something goes wrong, even when the month itself is covered.
pairs.reason: Someone who pays every bill but has no savings would not call themselves broke, and the alternative line for No savings makes that sharper.

pairs.distinction: Broke is money running short in general; Not enough food is the specific, sensitive moment when the shortage reaches the kitchen.
pairs.reason: Food running out needs its own fixes and, later, its own crisis resources, and a person living it would look for it by name rather than under Broke.

pairs.distinction: Broke is short on money now; Can't retire is a worry about the future, which people with a steady income have too.
pairs.reason: One is today and one is decades away, so nobody would confuse which of the two they are living with.
Worrying about my own food and seeing neighbors go hungry are the same pain seen from the personal and societal pages, so they stay two pains linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: No savings is having nothing put aside for any surprise; Medical bills is the cost of healthcare in particular, which can worry people who do have savings.
pairs.reason: A person choosing between them knows whether their worry is health costs or having no money set aside at all.

pairs.distinction: Scams is money I actually lost to someone who tricked me; Privacy is feeling watched by companies that collect my data.
pairs.reason: Losing money to a scammer and being tracked by companies are different experiences, and people would not mix them up.
